author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to pressure requirements.
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow during the cardiac cycle.

modules.description: Introduces the gross anatomy of the heart with a side-by-side intact and cutaway view, establishing anatomical orientation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize the external and internal gross anatomy of the heart.
Understand anatomical orientation conventions (patient's left/right vs viewer's left/right).
instructions: Use the rotate gesture to spin both heart models together.
Observe how left/right labeling corresponds to the patient's perspective, not the viewer's.

components.text: The Human Heart: Exterior and Interior Views

clips.changeMeaning: Initial spawn of the intact and cutaway heart models side by side with an overview title label, establishing the two views students will use throughout the module.
clips.narration: Welcome to the heart lab. Before you are two full-size models of the human heart. The one on your left is intact, showing its exterior surface and the great vessels. The one on your right is a cutaway, with the front wall removed to expose the interior chambers and valves. Both are oriented anatomically, with the apex pointing down and slightly to the left, just as it sits in the chest.

components.text: Patient's Right <-> Your Left | Patient's Left <-> Your Right

clips.changeMeaning: Adds orientation labels clarifying patient-perspective left/right convention and enables free rotation of both models for exploration.
clips.narration: Notice that the heart is described from the patient's own point of view, not yours. So the structures you see on your left as you look at these models are actually the heart's right side, and vice versa. This convention is used throughout anatomy and medicine. Try rotating the models to view them from different angles.

modules.description: A guided tour highlighting the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels in sequence, mapping interior cutaway structures to exterior landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers of the heart in circulatory order.
Name the four valves and the chambers/vessels they connect.
Name the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
instructions: Follow along as each structure is highlighted and labeled.
Compare the highlighted region on the cutaway view to the corresponding landmark on the intact view.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the right atrium on the cutaway model with a color tint and updates the floating label to name it.
clips.narration: Let's begin the structural tour with the four chambers. First, the right atrium, which receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts highlight and label from right atrium to right ventricle to continue the sequential chamber tour.
clips.narration: Next, the right ventricle, which receives blood from the right atrium and pumps it toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts highlight and label to the left atrium, progressing through the four-chamber sequence.
clips.narration: Now the left atrium, which receives freshly oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts highlight and label to the left ventricle, completing the four-chamber portion of the tour.
clips.narration: And finally the left ventricle, the heart's strongest chamber, which pumps oxygenated blood out to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions the tour from chambers to valves, highlighting the tricuspid valve location between right atrium and ventricle.
clips.narration: Now let's identify the four valves. First, the tricuspid valve, located between the right atrium and right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary valve, continuing the valve sequence.
clips.narration: Next, the pulmonary or pulmonic valve, between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the mitral/bicuspid valve and notes its dual naming convention for clinical relevance.
clips.narration: The mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. You will encounter both names in clinical practice.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the aortic valve, completing the four-valve portion of the tour.
clips.narration: And the aortic valve, between the left ventricle and the aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions tour to major vessels, beginning with the superior vena cava, highlighted on both cutaway and intact models.
clips.narration: Finally, let's look at the major vessels. The superior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from the upper body into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the inferior vena cava on both models, continuing the vessel sequence.
clips.narration: The inferior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from the lower body into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary arteries, noting they carry deoxygenated blood despite being arteries.
clips.narration: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary veins, contrasting them with the pulmonary arteries in oxygenation state.
clips.narration: The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the aorta on both models, concluding the vessel tour and the full structural inventory.
clips.narration: And finally, the aorta, the largest artery in the body, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle out to the systemic circulation.

modules.description: Visualizes the continuous dual-loop circulation with color-coded blood streams and highlights the pulmonary and systemic circuits as distinct units.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish oxygenated from deoxygenated blood using the red/blue color convention.
Identify the pulmonary circuit and systemic circuit as two distinct loops driven by the heart.
instructions: Observe the continuous flow of color through the cutaway heart.
Watch as the pulmonary and systemic circuits are highlighted individually.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the animated blood flow stream through the cutaway heart, establishing the red/blue color convention for oxygenation state.
clips.narration: Now watch as the heart fills with continuous, flowing color. Blue represents deoxygenated blood, found on the right side of the heart, in the pulmonary arteries, and in the systemic veins. Red represents oxygenated blood, found on the left side of the heart, in the pulmonary veins, and in the systemic arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights only the pulmonary circuit portion of the flow stream to isolate it as a distinct loop for student focus.
clips.narration: The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood and pumps it to the lungs. This loop, from the right ventricle through the lungs and back to the left atrium, is the pulmonary circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts highlight from the pulmonary circuit to the systemic circuit, showing the second loop of the dual circulation as a distinct unit.
clips.narration: The left side of the heart handles oxygenated blood and pumps it to the body. This loop, from the left ventricle through the systemic vessels and back to the right atrium, is the systemic circuit.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: An interactive step-through trace of a single red blood cell traveling the complete path through the heart and both circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the complete step-by-step path of blood through the heart's chambers, valves, and vessels.
Identify the point in the circuit where deoxygenated blood becomes oxygenated.
instructions: Press Next to advance the blood cell one step along its path.
Replay the trace as many times as you like to reinforce the sequence.

clips.changeMeaning: Places the blood cell at its starting position in the superior vena cava with an introductory label.
clips.narration: A single red blood cell begins its journey in the superior vena cava, carrying carbon dioxide from the body back toward the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the blood cell from the superior vena cava into the right atrium and updates the label to match.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the blood cell into the right ventricle after passing the tricuspid valve.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, pushing the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the blood cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries en route to the lungs.
clips.narration: The cell exits through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, then travels through the pulmonary arteries toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions the blood cell color from blue to red to represent gas exchange occurring in the lung capillaries.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, the cell releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen, changing from blue to red.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the newly oxygenated blood cell through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.
clips.narration: Now oxygenated, the cell returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the blood cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
clips.narration: The left atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the blood cell through the aortic valve into the aorta, exiting toward systemic circulation.
clips.narration: The powerful left ventricle contracts, pushing the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Completes the full circuit by returning the blood cell to its starting position and color, closing the loop for replay.
clips.narration: The cell travels through the body, delivers oxygen to the tissues, picks up carbon dioxide, and turns blue again as it returns through the systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the loop.

modules.description: Side-by-side cross-sections compare the myocardial wall thickness of the right and left ventricles, linking structure to pressure demands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the relative myocardial wall thickness of the right and left ventricles.
Explain the functional reason for the thickness asymmetry in terms of pulmonary versus systemic pressure demands.
instructions: Rotate each cross-section to inspect wall thickness from different angles.
Compare the scale markers on each cross-section directly.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two ventricular cross-sections side by side for direct visual comparison of myocardial wall thickness.
clips.narration: Here we see two cross-sections of the heart, cut at the same horizontal level through the ventricles. On the left is the right ventricle, and on the right is the left ventricle. Notice the difference in wall thickness even before we add measurements.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds a scale marker and label to the right ventricle cross-section indicating its thin wall thickness.
clips.narration: The right ventricle's myocardium is thin, roughly three to five millimeters in a healthy adult, because it only needs to pump blood a short distance to the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds a scale marker and label to the left ventricle cross-section indicating its thicker wall, completing the direct thickness comparison.
clips.narration: The left ventricle's myocardium is substantially thicker, roughly ten to fifteen millimeters, because it must generate enough pressure to pump blood through the entire body's systemic circulation, against much higher resistance.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: Demonstrates the open and closed states of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves and explains their role in preventing backflow during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish atrioventricular valves from semilunar valves by location and function.
Describe how valve open/closed states correspond to phases of ventricular contraction and relaxation.
instructions: Step through each valve's open and closed states.
Note which valves are open and which are closed during each phase of the cardiac cycle.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two valve categories and highlights the atrioventricular valves as the first focus of the demonstration.
clips.narration: There are two categories of valves. The atrioventricular valves, the tricuspid and mitral, sit between the atria and ventricles. The semilunar valves, the pulmonary and aortic, sit between the ventricles and their outflow arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps the AV valve model from open to closed to demonstrate leaflet sealing during ventricular contraction.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, the atrioventricular valves close to prevent blood from flowing backward into the atria. Here we see the tricuspid valve's leaflets sealed shut.

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps in the open valve model to represent the semilunar valves opening simultaneously with AV valve closure during contraction.
clips.narration: Meanwhile, the semilunar valves, the pulmonary and aortic, are open during this same phase, allowing blood to exit the ventricles into the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

components.text: AV Valves Open / Semilunar Valves Closed (Relaxation)

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps valve states again to show the reverse configuration during ventricular relaxation, completing the demonstration of both cardiac phases.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, the reverse occurs: the semilunar valves close to prevent blood from flowing back into the ventricles, while the atrioventricular valves open to allow the ventricles to refill.

modules.description: An unlabeled cutaway heart is shown with structures highlighted one at a time; students select the correct name from candidate options.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Correctly identify chambers, valves, and vessels of the heart without label assistance.
instructions: Select the correct name for each highlighted structure from the options presented.
Replay the quiz to reinforce identification skills.

components.text: What structure is highlighted? (Options: Right Atrium, Left Atrium, Right Ventricle, Aorta)

clips.changeMeaning: Removes labels from the cutaway heart and highlights the right atrium in yellow as the first quiz question, presenting answer options.
clips.narration: All labels have been removed. A structure will be highlighted in yellow. Choose the correct name from the options below.

components.text: What structure is highlighted? (Options: Tricuspid Valve, Mitral Valve, Pulmonary Valve, Aortic Valve)

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the correct answer for the right atrium and moves the highlight to the next structure (tricuspid valve) with new options.
clips.narration: Correct, that is the right atrium. Let's move on to the next structure, highlighted now.

components.text: What structure is highlighted? (Options: Pulmonary Arteries, Pulmonary Veins, Aorta, Vena Cava)

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the quiz to a vessel-identification question, highlighting the pulmonary arteries and presenting commonly confused options.
clips.narration: This next structure is one of the great vessels. Choose carefully between the pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins, since it's easy to confuse them.

modules.description: Students are given a starting position in the circulatory path and must select the correct next structure, reinforcing sequence and oxygenation distinctions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Correctly sequence the path of blood through the complete pulmonary and systemic circuit.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins based on the blood they carry.
instructions: Read the starting position and select the correct next structure in the path of blood flow.
Pay close attention to the direction of flow, especially around the lungs.

components.text: Blood has just entered the right atrium. What comes next?
Blood entered the right atrium. Next? (Tricuspid Valve, Mitral Valve, Pulmonary Valve, Aorta)

clips.changeMeaning: Presents the first flow-tracing question starting at the right atrium with candidate next structures.
clips.narration: A unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. What structure does it pass through next?

components.text: Blood is in the right ventricle. Next? (Pulmonary Valve, Mitral Valve, Aortic Valve, Vena Cava)

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the quiz to the next step, now asking what follows the right ventricle in the circulatory path.
clips.narration: Correct, the tricuspid valve. Now the blood is in the right ventricle. What structure does it pass through next?

components.text: After the lungs, oxygenated blood returns via? (Pulmonary Veins, Pulmonary Arteries, Vena Cava, Aorta)

clips.changeMeaning: Tests the common point of confusion between pulmonary arteries and veins by asking which vessel returns oxygenated blood from the lungs.
clips.narration: Correct. After the pulmonary valve, blood enters the pulmonary trunk and travels through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Remember, these arteries carry deoxygenated blood, unlike systemic arteries. After gas exchange, which vessel carries the now-oxygenated blood back to the heart?

modules.description: A summary screen reviews the five concept areas covered in the lab, highlighting each in turn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Review and consolidate the five major concept areas covered in the lab: structural inventory, dual-circuit organization, blood path tracing, wall thickness asymmetry, and valve function.
instructions: Listen to the recap as each concept area is highlighted in sequence.

components.text:
1. Chambers, Valves, Vessels
2. Dual-Circuit Circulation
3. Path of a Blood Cell
4. Wall Thickness Asymmetry
5. Valve Function

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the first recap item, the structural inventory of chambers, valves, and vessels, in the summary list.
clips.narration: Let's review what we've covered. First, the structural inventory: the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels of the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts emphasis to the second recap item, dual-circuit organization of pulmonary and systemic circulation.
clips.narration: Second, the dual-circuit organization: the pulmonary circuit carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the systemic circuit carrying oxygenated blood to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts emphasis to the third recap item, the traced path of blood through the full circuit.
clips.narration: Third, the complete path of a unit of blood through the full circuit, from superior vena cava back to the aorta and beyond.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts emphasis to the fourth recap item, ventricular wall thickness asymmetry and its functional basis.
clips.narration: Fourth, the wall thickness asymmetry between the left and right ventricles, reflecting the differing pressure demands of the systemic and pulmonary circuits.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts emphasis to the fifth and final recap item, valve function, and closes out the lab summary.
clips.narration: And fifth, the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow throughout the cardiac cycle. Congratulations, you've completed the heart anatomy and circulation lab.
